summary: This informational document identifies failure cases that IPv6-enabled mobile customers can hit while roaming. The analysis finds the causes include improper configurations, incomplete feature support in equipment, and incompatibilities between networks.

eli5.summary: Using your phone abroad can break when the networks are set up differently. This note lists the ways it can go wrong with the newer internet addresses.

questions: why does ipv6 fail when roaming
how to support ipv6 in roaming networks
subtitle: Why mobile customers lose IPv6 connectivity when roaming abroad

tldr.problem: Mobile customers roaming to different operators' networks often experience service disruptions when trying to use IPv6, even though both home and visited networks support it.
tldr.mechanism: The document analyzes failure points across three stages: network attachment (device joining a visited network), PDP/PDN context creation (IP address allocation), and service requests (applications using the connection).
tldr.outcome: Operators must align roaming agreements, update equipment to support dual-stack bearers, and implement proper user profile configurations to ensure consistent IPv6 availability across home and visited networks.

today: RFC 7445 is an Informational document that documents known problems in IPv6 roaming deployments. It has not been obsoleted. Operators continue to use its guidance to avoid roaming failures when deploying IPv6.

sections.title: Understanding IPv6 Roaming
sections.content:
Mobile operators worldwide have deployed or are deploying IPv6 in their networks. A mobile device with IPv6 support should be able to receive IPv6 connectivity in either a home network or a visited network when roaming internationally. However, real-world deployments show that roaming customers often experience service disruptions due to inconsistent configurations, incomplete equipment support, and incompatibilities between how different networks handle IPv6.

The document focuses on the 3GPP mobile networks used worldwide (2G, 3G, and 4G). It identifies specific failure cases that occur in three distinct stages of a roaming connection: network attachment, IP address allocation, and service requests.
sections.eli5: When you roam to a new country, your phone has to identify itself, get an IP address, and then run apps. At each of these stages, things can break if the home and visited networks don't agree on how to handle IPv6.

sections.title: How Roaming Connections Work
sections.content:
There are two main roaming architectures. In home-routed mode, the roaming device gets all its IP addresses from the home network, and all traffic is routed back through home network equipment. This requires transit networks (GRX/IPX) between home and visited networks and simplifies charging but adds latency.

In local breakout mode, the visited network assigns IP addresses directly and routes traffic locally. This is faster and more efficient but requires the visited network to support the same features as the home network. It is increasingly used for services like VoLTE (voice calls over 4G) to reduce latency.

Before either mode can work, the device must complete network attachment, where the visited network authenticates the subscriber and downloads their profile from the home network's subscriber database (HLR/HSS). The profile lists allowed IP types (IPv4, IPv6, or both) and which roaming mode to use.
sections.eli5: Your home network can either handle all your traffic (like routing every postcard back home) or let the visited network handle it locally (like mailing it from where you are). Before either works, the visited network checks who you are by calling your home network.

sections.title: Failures at Network Attachment
sections.content:
The first critical failure point is when the device joins the visited network. Modern 3GPP standards define a PDP/PDN Type IPv4v6 that allows one connection to carry both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses. However, older 2G and 3G equipment, particularly Serving GPRS Support Nodes (SGSN) before Release 9, does not recognize this type.

When an old SGSN receives a subscriber profile containing the IPv4v6 type, it cannot correctly process the field (ext-pdp-Type) and may discard the entire attachment request instead of ignoring the unknown field. This violates 3GPP standards, which require devices to silently skip unsupported fields.

To avoid this, operators must update roaming agreements to ensure visited SGSN nodes support dual-stack, or implement non-standard logic in the home network's HLR/HSS to send IPv4-only or IPv6-only profiles to known legacy equipment.
sections.eli5: Old network equipment doesn't understand the instruction for both IPv4 and IPv6 together. Instead of ignoring it, the equipment rejects your phone entirely. The home network has to be smart enough to send different instructions to old versus new equipment.

sections.title: Failures During IP Address Allocation
sections.content:
Once attached, the device requests an IP address context (PDP/PDN context). Several failures can occur here:

Case 1: Bearer splitting. A device asking for both IPv4 and IPv6 in one connection (IPv4v6) may encounter a visited network that only supports single-stack bearers. The network rejects the request and causes the device to create two separate connections—one for IPv4, one for IPv6. This doubles resource consumption and can exceed device limits or hit network policies that allow only one connection per subscriber.

Case 2: IPv6 unsupported. Some visited networks allow only IPv4 activation or do not enable IPv6 on their equipment by default. An IPv6-only device simply fails to get any connectivity.

Case 3: Wrong APN configuration. If the home network uses IPv6-only for home-routed connections but the device roams to a local-breakout APN that defaults to IPv4, the request fails because the APN's allowed types do not match what the device requested.

Case 4: No fallback. In local breakout, a device requesting pure IPv6 may receive only IPv4 from the visited network. Without a standard fallback mechanism, the device loses connectivity rather than using the IPv4 address.
sections.eli5: If the network can't give you what you asked for (like IPv6), it either splits your request into two connections, rejects it, or tries to swap it for something else. Any of these can break your access to the internet.

sections.title: Failures at the Service Layer
sections.content:
After obtaining an IP connection, applications request services. Two issues commonly arise:

IPv6-unaware applications: In local breakout mode with IPv6-only assignments (common for IMS services like VoLTE in roaming), applications that only understand IPv4 will not work. Translation mechanisms like 464XLAT (IPv4-to-IPv6 translation with NAT64) can help, but require that the visited network deploy both NAT64 and DNS64 devices.

464XLAT failures: Even when translation is available, the client-side translator (CLAT) on the device must discover the server-side translator's (PLAT) IPv6 prefix. If the visited network lacks DNS64 or NAT64, or if a pre-configured prefix in the CLAT does not match the PLAT's actual prefix, translation fails. The device then cannot reach IPv4 servers.
sections.eli5: Even after you have an IP address, apps may not know how to use IPv6. Translators can help, but both sides must be set up correctly or they fail.

sections.title: Recommended Configurations and Solutions
sections.content:
The document suggests several approaches to reduce failures:

For network attachment: Roaming agreements should mandate that visited operators update SGSN firmware to Release 9 or later, or the home operator should implement logic to detect legacy equipment and send it IPv4-only or IPv6-only profiles instead of IPv4v6.

For IP allocation: In home-routed mode, the home network should ensure its APN profiles use IPv4v6 and the visited SGSN should set the Dual Address Bearer Flag (DAF). In local breakout mode, operators may configure a dedicated APN that requests only IPv4 to avoid bearer splitting. Alternatively, operators can set the device to IPv4-only when roaming locally.

For service requests: In local breakout with IPv6-only, operators can deploy 464XLAT translation. Alternatively, they can use home-routed mode instead, or allow devices to use different profiles (IPv4-only when roaming, dual-stack at home).

User profile provisioning: The HLR/HSS should support multiple context profiles with the same ID but different IP types, allowing the network to select the right profile based on detected equipment capabilities.
sections.eli5: Networks need to agree on rules, update old equipment, and sometimes send different instructions to different places. Or they can stay simple and use just IPv4 when roaming, and dual-stack at home.
